newsitem.title: INDIA: Sweden's Tetra Pak to invest $40 million in India.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's Tetra Pak to invest $40 million in India.

text.p: Swedish packaging giant Tetra Pak on Thursday inaugurated its first plant in India and announced plans to invest $40 million over the next few years, urging the government to widen reforms in the food-processing sector.
"The bulk of this will be concentrated in promoting the increased use of Tetra Pak in the dairy and liquid food processing industries," said Harry Salonaho, the firm's regional president.
He was speaking shortly after a function to inaugurate Tetra Pak's state-of-the-art plant at Takwe, near the western city of Pune close to Bombay.

Built at a cost of $17 million, the plant will produce rolls of the multilayered polyethyelene and aluminium foil packaging material that has revolutionised food processing techniques since its invention in 1951.

"India is the largest producer of milk in the world," said Goran Grosskopf, chairman of the parent Tetra Laval group, "but it is one of the lowest consumers of the milk. Tetra Pak will help to change that."

Tetra Pak officials said they saw a major opportunity in helping to transport perishable foods across vast distances from the rural areas where the bulk of the production is carried out, to consumers in urban locations hundreds of miles away.
"India is one of the largest producers of fruit, but about 30 percent of it is wasted because of the lack of processing, packaging and distribution facilities," Grosskopf said.

India is the world's largest producer of fruits, and its second largest cultivator of vegetables. The country's annual fruit production, at 33 million tonnes, accounts for about 8.6 percent of global production, company officials said.
It also accounts for 15 percent of the world's production of vegetables, an estimated 71 million tonnes, the company said in a statement.
"Wastage amounts to a loss of over $1.5 billion," it added.
Grosskopf called on the Indian government to accelerate its deregulation policies to the areas of food processing as well.
India threw open many sectors of its economy to foreign private enterprise in 1991, as part of a programme of economic reform that tore down decades-old protectionist barriers.

"The opening up of the economy, the liberalisation of companies, the cancellation of lots of import duties, the building up of infrastructure -- all these steps are necessary to build up India as a developed nation of the world," Grosskopf said.

The Indian governments' present policy of putting constraints on the agro-processing industry in terms of capacity, collection and procurement areas, high tariffs on the import of capital goods has hampered the growth of the sector, the company statement said.

"Several companies, both Indian as well as transnational, are keen to make large investments. What is needed is the right kind of policy framework for their entry and continued operation," Grosskopf said.

Tetra Pak acquired Swiss engineering group Alfa Laval in 1991. The company statement said Tetra Pak had a turnover of 7.9 billion Swiss francs in 1995. That year it produced packaging that delivered 44.7 billion litres of liquid food products.
